title: Yom Kippur: the gates close
hookLine: the day opens with Kol Nidre and ends as the gates of prayer close

cards: Yom Kippur opens with a melody and closes with a horn. At sunset, the synagogue is packed.
The Torah scrolls are taken out and held, and a cantor sings a haunting old melody three times, each time a little louder: Kol Nidre.

Then, a whole day later, as the light starts to fade and everyone is hungry, tired and still standing, the last prayer begins. The doors of the ark stay open. People who sat through the afternoon get to their feet.
They know what time it is.

teach.b: First, the opening. Kol Nidre means all vows. It isn't really a prayer; it's a legal formula in Aramaic, releasing the vows a person makes to God and can't keep.
Jewish law is clear: it doesn't cancel promises made to other people; those have to be kept or made right with the person.
Its power is the melody and the moment: a whole community admitting that people promise more than they manage. Now the end.
The final service is called Neilah, which means locking, or closing. The rabbis remembered a closing prayer in the Temple, said as the great gates were locked at sunset.
They also spoke of the gates of heaven, open all day to prayer, now swinging shut. So Neilah feels like the last minutes before a door closes.
All through these days, the prayers have asked God to write us in the book of life. In Neilah, the word changes: seal us. The writing is almost done.
Then the ending comes all at once. The congregation says the Shema, once. Then, three times, the line that follows it: blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever.
Then, seven times, the words the people cried out on Mount Carmel in Elijah's day: "The LORD, He is God."

teach.h: THE SHEMA, AND ONE LONG BLAST.
teach.b: And one long blast of the shofar.
The fast is over. Many say next year in Jerusalem, and go home to eat. That closes a week of Modeh Ani, the calendar, the new moon, the shofar, the river, the fast, and now the gates.

how: Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, chanted three times at sunset, and ends with Neilah, prayed standing before the open ark. It closes with the Shema, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, and a long blast of the shofar.

games.q: it's the last hour of Yom Kippur. you're hungry and tired, and Neilah is starting. the ark is open. what does the custom suggest?
o: slip out early to beat the crowd.
sit quietly and wait for the shofar.
games.why: the custom is to stand through Neilah while the ark is open: the last minutes before the gates close, when the prayers change from write us to seal us.

practice: Imagine the day is almost over and the gates are closing: what's the one thing you'd still want to say, to God if you pray, to someone you love, or to yourself?
Keep it to one sentence, and let it get simpler with each breath until it's only a few words.
